title: Coriolanus
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Rome in the first years of the Republic, with the Volscian towns of Corioli and Antium
lengthNote: Around 3,750 lines in the Globe text, among the longest of the tragedies
openingLine: Before we proceed any further, hear me speak.
summary: A city short of grain makes a soldier its hero and then asks him to stand in the marketplace, show his scars and ask for votes. He can take a walled town almost single-handed and cannot say a civil sentence to a citizen, so Rome banishes him and he brings the enemy back to its gates. The play gives the crowd real arguments, gives the hero none worth having, and then hands the ending to his mother.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Coriolanus
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. The only early text is the First Folio, which carries unusually detailed stage directions.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Shakespeare's last Roman play, and probably his last tragedy.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: Folio only. Its stage directions are fuller than usual, which is why the silence in 5.3 carries so much weight.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: Whole speeches are lifted from the Life of Caius Martius Coriolanus and turned into verse with minimal alteration.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Act I alone has ten, most of them short: the battle for Corioli is cut like a sequence of dispatches.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A grain riot, and a war that solves it
structure.summary: Citizens with clubs come out over the price of corn and are answered with a fable about a belly. Marcius insults them, the senate grants them tribunes anyway, and then a Volscian war conveniently arrives. He takes Corioli almost alone, is renamed for the city he captured, and refuses his share of the spoils.

scenes.title: Corn at our own price
scenes.summary: The citizens rise over grain; Menenius tells the fable of the belly; Marcius arrives and calls them scabs.

scenes.title: Corioli
scenes.summary: Aufidius learns that Rome knows his plans and says he wants Marcius in the field.

scenes.title: The women at home
scenes.summary: Volumnia rejoices in her son's wounds; Virgilia will not leave the house until he returns.

scenes.title: The gates
scenes.summary: Marcius curses his own retreating soldiers and is shut inside the town alone.

scenes.title: Inside the walls
scenes.summary: Romans loot while Marcius, still bleeding, goes to find Cominius.

scenes.title: Make you a sword of me
scenes.summary: He asks for volunteers and is taken up in the arms of the whole army.

scenes.title: A garrison left
scenes.summary: Lartius secures Corioli and follows to the field.

scenes.title: Marcius and Aufidius
scenes.summary: The two meet in single combat and are parted by Volscian soldiers.

scenes.title: The name
scenes.summary: He refuses the tenth of the spoils, is hailed Coriolanus, and forgets the name of a poor host he wanted pardoned.

scenes.title: Aufidius vows
scenes.summary: Beaten five times, Aufidius says he will have Marcius by any means, honourable or not.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The gown of humility
structure.summary: Rome welcomes him back with a noise that frightens the tribunes, and the senate offers the consulship. Custom requires him to stand in the Forum in a plain gown, show his wounds and ask each citizen for a voice. He gets the votes by sneering through the ceremony, and the tribunes go to work on the men who gave them.

scenes.title: The return
scenes.summary: Menenius baits the tribunes; Volumnia counts her son's wounds before he arrives.

scenes.title: The Capitol
scenes.summary: Cominius reports his deeds while Coriolanus walks out rather than hear them praised.

scenes.title: The Forum
scenes.summary: He asks for voices, receives them, and the tribunes persuade the citizens to take them back.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Banished
structure.summary: Told his election is revoked, he says in public what the patricians say in private: that giving the people a share in power will destroy the state. The tribunes call it treason and stage a trial. Volumnia persuades him to go and apologise; he lasts a few lines before the word 'traitor' undoes the performance, and Rome expels him.

scenes.title: The street
scenes.summary: Coriolanus argues for abolishing the tribunate and is nearly seized on the spot.

scenes.title: His mother's instruction
scenes.summary: Volumnia teaches him how to perform humility; he agrees to try.

scenes.title: The Forum again
scenes.summary: Provoked by the charge of treason, he curses the city and banishes it from himself.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: A world elsewhere
structure.summary: He parts from his family at the gate with unexpected gentleness, and walks to Antium in disguise to offer his throat to his oldest enemy. Aufidius embraces him, gives him half the army, and then watches his own officers begin to prefer the newcomer. The Volscian force moves on Rome and the tribunes discover what they have arranged.

scenes.title: The parting
scenes.summary: He comforts his mother and wife at the city gate and leaves alone.

scenes.title: Anger's my meat
scenes.summary: Volumnia meets the tribunes in the street and curses them with an appetite of her own.

scenes.title: A road
scenes.summary: A Roman spy and a Volscian exchange news of the banishment and the mobilisation.

scenes.title: Antium
scenes.summary: Disguised outside Aufidius's house, he reflects on how quickly friends turn enemies.

scenes.title: The offer
scenes.summary: He names himself, offers his throat, and is given half the Volscian command.

scenes.title: Rome hears
scenes.summary: The tribunes are congratulating themselves on a quiet city when the news arrives.

scenes.title: Aufidius reconsiders
scenes.summary: His lieutenant reports that the soldiers now follow Coriolanus; Aufidius begins to plan.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The silence, and what follows it
structure.summary: Cominius and Menenius are sent to plead and are turned away. Then his mother, wife and son come, and Volumnia argues, kneels and finally stops. He takes her hand and says nothing for as long as the scene will hold, then grants the peace and tells her what it will cost him. Aufidius kills him in Corioli, over a name.

scenes.title: Menenius is persuaded to go
scenes.summary: Cominius reports that Coriolanus would not answer to his own name.

scenes.title: The sentry
scenes.summary: Menenius is refused at the guard post and sent back to Rome.

scenes.title: The embassy of women
scenes.summary: Volumnia, Virgilia and Young Marcius kneel; he holds her hand, silent, and yields.

scenes.title: Rome waits
scenes.summary: Menenius describes a man grown from grub to dragon; the city hears the news and goes out to meet Volumnia.

scenes.title: The mother welcomed
scenes.summary: Rome honours the women as its deliverers.

scenes.title: Corioli
scenes.summary: Aufidius calls him boy and traitor; the conspirators kill him, and then carry the body out with honour.

characters.name: Caius Marcius Coriolanus
characters.role: A Roman patrician and general, named for the city he captured
characters.summary: He is superb at the one thing Rome no longer principally needs and incapable of the thing it now requires. His refusal to display his wounds or ask for votes is usually read as pride, but it is also a refusal to let his body be turned into an argument, which is the only consistent principle he has.
characters.clue: He takes a walled town almost single-handed, and cannot get through a five-minute conversation with the men whose votes he needs.
traits: unable to be flattered or to flatter

relationships.label: son of
relationships.note: She made him, tells him so, and uses the fact twice.

characters.name: Volumnia
characters.summary: She built him: she says she sent him to a cruel war when he was still a boy and would rather have eleven sons die nobly than one live idly. She is also the best politician in the play, and the one person who understands that the Forum requires acting — which is why her final speech works and destroys him at the same time.
characters.clue: She would rather see her son's forehead bleeding than a trophy gilded, and she teaches him to bow to a crowd she despises as thoroughly as he does.
traits: victorious at a price she names

characters.name: Virgilia
characters.summary: She is the play's other kind of attachment: where Volumnia counts wounds, Virgilia refuses to leave the house until her husband is home and cannot bear the word blood. Her husband calls her his gracious silence, and in 5.3 she speaks eleven words that reach him before any of his mother's rhetoric does.
characters.clue: She will not cross her own threshold while her husband is at the war, and her tears succeed where an argument has not.

characters.name: Menenius Agrippa
characters.role: A patrician, and Coriolanus's oldest friend in Rome
characters.summary: He handles the crowd with jokes and a fable about the belly, which is the most sophisticated piece of political management in the play and also a way of telling hungry men that the distribution is natural. His confidence that the general will listen to him is the play's cruellest small humiliation.
characters.clue: He answers a riot about the price of grain with a story about the stomach and the other parts of the body.

characters.name: Tullus Aufidius
characters.summary: He is the only man in the play who values Coriolanus at his own valuation, which is why exile takes him to Antium rather than anywhere else. The embrace in 4.5 is in the language of a wedding night, and by 4.7 he is already calculating how to be rid of a guest who has taken his army's affection.
characters.clue: He dreams of his enemy, welcomes him into his house with more warmth than he showed his bride, and has him stabbed in a public place.

characters.name: Sicinius Velutus
characters.summary: He reads a crowd the way a general reads ground, and knows that the surest way to defeat a candidate is to let him speak. His question in 3.1 — what is the city but the people? — is the clearest statement of republican principle anyone makes, and he makes it while managing a prosecution.
characters.clue: He asks what a city is if not its people, and then coaches those people on exactly when to shout.
traits: principled and manipulative in the same breath

characters.name: Junius Brutus
characters.summary: The quieter half of the pair, and the one who does the detailed work: rehearsing the citizens on what they should have said, choosing the moment to say the word traitor. He is right that a consul who wants to abolish the tribunate is a danger to the people who elected him.
characters.clue: He tells the citizens what they ought to have replied in the Forum, then sends them back to unsay their votes.

characters.name: Cominius
characters.role: Consul and general of the Roman army
characters.summary: He gives the long report of Marcius's deeds at the Capitol, which is the only place in the play where the hero's worth is set out at length by someone who was there. In Act V he comes back from the Volscian camp with the detail that says everything: the man would not answer to his own name.
characters.clue: He praises a soldier who walks out rather than hear it, and returns from an embassy to report that the man no longer answers to any name at all.

characters.name: The Citizens of Rome
characters.role: The plebeians, who riot, vote and banish
characters.summary: Shakespeare gives them numbered voices with different opinions, so they argue with each other before anyone argues with them. They are mocked for changing their minds, and the play is careful to show exactly who worked on them each time they did.
characters.clue: They come on with clubs over the price of corn, grant a man their voices in the Forum, and take them back before the scene is over.

themes.name: Hunger and the distribution of grain
themes.summary: The play opens with men who want corn at their own price, not with an abstraction about liberty, and it never lets the political argument float free of that. Menenius answers a material complaint with a story about the body's parts working together, which is a good fable and a bad answer, and the play says so by keeping the citizens hungry.
themes.development: The riot in 1.1 is settled by the grant of tribunes; the corn arrives from Greece by 3.1, where Coriolanus objects that it was given free to men who did not earn it.

themes.name: Voices and consent
themes.summary: The word 'voices' means votes, and Coriolanus repeats it until it stops meaning anything, which is precisely his problem with it: he hears noise where the constitution hears consent. Rome's new arrangement requires the powerful to ask, and he would rather starve than crave the hire he thinks he has already earned.
themes.development: He collects voices in 2.3 with open contempt, the tribunes teach the citizens to withdraw them, and by 3.3 the same voices are a cry of curs that he claims to banish.

themes.name: The body and the body politic
themes.summary: Rome is described as a body from the first scene, and the metaphor is never allowed to stay comfortable: a belly that hoards, a great toe that leads a rebellion, wounds that must be shown in public, scars counted by a mother at home. What the state wants from Coriolanus is his body as evidence, and that is the one thing he will not surrender.
themes.development: Menenius's fable in 1.1 is answered by the demand for wounds in 2.3, and by Volumnia in 5.3 asking him to tread on the womb that bore him.

themes.name: Mother and son
themes.summary: Volumnia states plainly that she made her son what he is, and the play offers no competing account of where his valour came from. The tragedy is not that he disobeys her but that he obeys twice: once in 3.2, when she teaches him to act, and once in 5.3, when the acting has to stop.
themes.development: She counts his wounds in 2.1, coaches him in 3.2, and in 5.3 wins the argument and, by his own statement, kills him with it.

themes.name: Names and what they cost
themes.summary: He is given a new name for a city he took and has to be told what it is; he then discovers that the name is a possession which can be used against him. By Act V he will not answer to it, and in the last scene he is killed for insisting on it in front of the men he took it from.
themes.development: He is hailed Coriolanus in 1.9, cannot recall the name of the man he wanted saved, refuses his own name in 5.1, and dies reciting the deed it commemorates in 5.6.

themes.name: Public performance and integrity
themes.summary: The gown of humility is a costume, the Forum is a stage, and everyone except Coriolanus can see that this is not a scandal but the ordinary condition of public life. His refusal to act looks like the play's only honesty, until his mother points out that he has been playing a part called 'the man I am' all along.
themes.development: He cannot perform in 2.3, agrees to try in 3.2 and fails within twenty lines in 3.3; in 5.3 he says he has forgotten his part like a dull actor, and that is when he becomes human.

techniques.name: The political fable
techniques.definition: A story told to a crowd in order to settle an argument by analogy.
techniques.inThisBook: Menenius's belly and its rebellious members is lifted from the historical tradition, and Shakespeare stages the citizens interrupting it, so the audience sees the device being used and resisted at the same time.

techniques.name: Crowd scenes
techniques.definition: Staging a group as a set of distinct voices rather than a single mass.
techniques.inThisBook: The citizens are numbered, disagree with each other, and reason out loud before they act, which makes the patricians' contempt for them a claim the play can test.

techniques.name: Animal imagery
techniques.definition: Comparisons that place people on a scale from vermin to predators.
techniques.inThisBook: Curs, scabs, geese, hares, a lamb that baes like a bear, a grub that becomes a butterfly and a man who becomes a dragon: the insults define the political sides before the arguments do.

techniques.name: Imagery of the body
techniques.definition: The state described as anatomy, and anatomy treated as evidence.
techniques.inThisBook: Wounds are counted, displayed, refused and finally invoked in 5.3, so the same body that took Corioli becomes the disputed ground of the political plot.

techniques.name: The significant stage direction
techniques.definition: A moment of action written into the text with no words attached to it.
techniques.inThisBook: 'He holds her by the hand, silent' is the most famous direction in Shakespeare, and it gives the turning point of the tragedy to a pause rather than a speech.

techniques.name: Heroic hyperbole
techniques.definition: Description inflated past the plausible in order to make a man into a monument.
techniques.inThisBook: Cominius reports a soldier who entered a city alone and came out painted with blood; the play keeps the language of epic while showing us the ordinary politics it cannot survive.

quotations.text: Before we proceed any further, hear me speak.
quotations.speaker: First Citizen
quotations.context: The opening line of the play, spoken by a citizen carrying a club.
quotations.analysis: No Shakespearean tragedy begins with a commoner claiming the floor, and the claim is procedural: he is asking for order before an action, not for pity. The whole play is contained in the request, because the one thing Coriolanus will never grant the citizens is the right to be heard before anything proceeds.

quotations.text: There was a time when all the body's members Rebell'd against the belly, thus accused it: That only like a gulf it did remain I' the midst o' the body, idle and unactive, Still cupboarding the viand, never bearing Like labour with the rest,
quotations.speaker: Menenius
quotations.context: Talking a crowd of hungry men out of a riot over the price of corn.
quotations.analysis: The fable answers a complaint about hoarding by conceding the hoarding and calling it digestion. Its rhetorical trick is the opening 'There was a time', which shifts the argument out of this year's harvest into a fable where the belly's case has already been settled — and the citizens interrupt him twice to say so.

quotations.text: What's the matter, you dissentious rogues, That, rubbing the poor itch of your opinion, Make yourselves scabs?
quotations.speaker: Caius Marcius
quotations.context: His entrance, immediately after Menenius has spent a hundred lines calming the crowd.
quotations.analysis: His first words undo the fable in three lines: where Menenius made the citizens limbs of a body, he makes them a skin disease on it. 'Opinion' is treated as an itch, which is to say a physical irritation with no content, and that is precisely his view of the vote he will later have to ask for.

quotations.text: He that will give good words to thee will flatter Beneath abhorring.
quotations.speaker: Caius Marcius
quotations.context: Answering a citizen who says they have always had his good word.
quotations.analysis: He treats courtesy to an inferior as a form of lying, which is consistent and politically fatal in equal measure. The line also explains why he cannot be bought: a man who regards flattery as beneath contempt has no currency to spend in a republic that runs on it.

quotations.text: Marcius, I had rather had eleven die nobly for their country than one voluptuously surfeit out of action.
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: In the house, sewing with Virgilia, on the subject of sons.
quotations.analysis: The arithmetic is the shock: eleven is not a figure of speech but a rate of exchange she has evidently worked out. 'Surfeit' plants the play's other appetite — the city outside is rioting over food — so her contempt for a well-fed son runs on the same imagery as the grain crisis.

quotations.text: it more becomes a man Than gilt his trophy: the breasts of Hecuba, When she did suckle Hector, look'd not lovelier Than Hector's forehead when it spit forth blood At Grecian sword, contemning.
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: Virgilia has just cried out at the thought of her husband's bloody brow.
quotations.analysis: The comparison sets a nursing mother against a wounded son and decides for the wound, which tells us exactly what kind of feeding Volumnia believes in. The verb 'spit' does the work: blood is given an agency and a contempt of its own, as though the forehead were answering the Greek sword back.

quotations.text: O, me alone! make you a sword of me? If these shows be not outward, which of you But is four Volsces?
quotations.speaker: Caius Marcius
quotations.context: The soldiers take him up in their arms and throw their caps in the air.
quotations.analysis: It is the one moment where a crowd loves him and he is delighted by it, which shows that his difficulty is not with numbers of people but with what those people are entitled to ask. Being made into a weapon is the only public use of his body that he can accept.

quotations.text: Nature teaches beasts to know their friends.
quotations.speaker: Sicinius
quotations.context: Sparring with Menenius in a public place while Rome waits for the victorious army.
quotations.analysis: Menenius answers by asking who the wolf loves, and the exchange turns into a small contest over who gets to use the animal metaphors. It is worth noticing that the tribunes are given the wit to hold their own here: the play does not write them as fools, only as men with an interest.

quotations.text: Bid them wash their faces And keep their teeth clean.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Asked what he shall say to the citizens who are coming to give him their voices.
quotations.analysis: Standing in the gown of humility, he answers a question about political speech with a note about hygiene, and the joke is directed at the audience rather than at anyone on stage. The contempt is specifically for their mouths — the parts that are about to give him what he needs.

quotations.text: Most sweet voices! Better it is to die, better to starve, Than crave the hire which first we do deserve.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Alone in the Forum, between groups of citizens.
quotations.analysis: The sarcasm of the first phrase gives way to a rhymed couplet, and the rhyme makes it a maxim he has clearly held for a long time. 'Starve' is a reckless word to choose in this city in this month, and the citizens who riot over corn in Act I are exactly the men whose hire he is refusing to crave.

quotations.text: What custom wills, in all things should we do't, The dust on antique time would lie unswept, And mountainous error be too highly heapt For truth to o'er-peer.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Still in the Forum, arguing himself out of completing the ceremony.
quotations.analysis: It is a genuinely radical argument — that custom preserves error — and it is being used to avoid asking poor men for their votes. The play repeatedly gives him positions that would be admirable in another mouth, which is what makes him a tragic figure rather than a snob.

quotations.text: For the mutable, rank-scented many, let them Regard me as I do not flatter, and Therein behold themselves:
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: In the street, after being told his election is revoked.
quotations.analysis: He offers his own refusal to flatter as a mirror in which the people may see their own inconstancy, which is an argument and an insult in the same sentence. 'Mutable' is the charge the play half sustains: the citizens do change their minds, and we have just watched two men talk them into it.

quotations.text: What is the city but the people?
quotations.speaker: Sicinius
quotations.context: In the street riot, as the tribunes move to arrest Coriolanus.
quotations.analysis: The citizens answer 'The people are the city', and the echo turns a rhetorical question into something closer to a chant. It is the most quotable line of political theory in the play, and Shakespeare gives it to a man in the middle of organising a lynching — which is not a refutation, only a complication.

quotations.text: Why did you wish me milder? would you have me False to my nature? Rather say I play The man I am.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: His mother has just told him he should have dissembled until he had the office.
quotations.analysis: He means 'play' as an accusation and it turns into a confession: the verb concedes that even being oneself is a performance. From this point the play measures him not by whether he acts but by which part he is willing to take, and in 5.3 he will use the language of the theatre again, as a man who has forgotten his lines.

quotations.text: Action is eloquence, and the eyes of the ignorant More learned than the ears--waving thy head, Which often, thus, correcting thy stout heart,
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: Teaching her son how to stand and what to do with his hands in front of the people.
quotations.analysis: She is giving him a lesson in stagecraft, complete with a demonstration of the gesture, and the phrase 'the eyes of the ignorant' shows she shares his contempt entirely. The difference between mother and son is not principle but competence: she can do the thing they both despise.

quotations.text: You common cry of curs! whose breath I hate As reek o' the rotten fens, whose loves I prize As the dead carcasses of unburied men That do corrupt my air, I banish you;
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Immediately after the tribunes pronounce his banishment in the Forum.
quotations.analysis: Everything he hates is airborne — breath, reek, corrupted air — which is the same sense in which their votes are only noise to him. Reversing the sentence is magnificent and changes nothing: a man can banish a city only from himself, and the city goes on without him for two more acts.

quotations.text: There is a world elsewhere.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: His exit line from Rome.
quotations.analysis: Five words to close an act, and the only thing in the speech that turns out to be true: there is a world elsewhere, and it is Antium, and it kills him. The plainness after twenty lines of curses is what makes it land — he stops performing for exactly one line.

quotations.text: Anger's my meat; I sup upon myself, And so shall starve with feeding.
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: In the street, having just cursed the tribunes who banished her son.
quotations.analysis: The play's food imagery finally reaches the patrician household: where the citizens wanted corn, she eats her own rage and expects to die of the diet. It is also an exact description of what she does to her son in 5.3, where feeding on him and destroying him are the same act.

quotations.text: One fire drives out one fire; one nail, one nail; Rights by rights falter, strengths by strengths do fail.
quotations.speaker: Aufidius
quotations.context: Alone with his lieutenant, having learned that the Volscian soldiers now prefer Coriolanus.
quotations.analysis: Two proverbs and a rhymed couplet, and the effect is of a man consoling himself with common sense while deciding on a murder. The symmetry of the second line — rights against rights, strengths against strengths — makes assassination sound like a law of physics rather than a choice.

quotations.text: let the Volsces Plough Rome and harrow Italy: I'll never Be such a gosling to obey instinct, but stand, As if a man were author of himself And knew no other kin.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Watching his mother, wife and son approach his tent, and steeling himself.
quotations.analysis: 'As if' gives him away before the sentence ends: he knows the self-authorship is a fiction he is choosing to act out. Four scenes after a mother's teaching failed to make him bow to a crowd, he is using her own vocabulary of performance to try to resist her.

quotations.text: Like a dull actor now, I have forgot my part, and I am out, Even to a full disgrace.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Virgilia has spoken three words to him and he cannot continue.
quotations.analysis: The man who refused to act in the Forum now describes his own collapse as a failure of acting, and 'out' is the technical term for an actor who has dried. His wife does it with a greeting; his mother will need fifty lines and a kneeling child.

quotations.text: Trust to't, thou shalt not--on thy mother's womb, That brought thee to this world.
quotations.speaker: Volumnia
quotations.context: Telling him he will not reach Rome except over her body.
quotations.analysis: She makes her own body the gate of the city, which completes the play's long argument that Rome is an anatomy. Virgilia and the boy each add a line immediately afterwards, so the threat arrives as a family in sequence rather than as one woman's rhetoric.

quotations.text: O mother, mother! What have you done? Behold, the heavens do ope, The gods look down, and this unnatural scene They laugh at.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Breaking the silence after holding his mother's hand without speaking.
quotations.analysis: The Folio's direction — he holds her by the hand, silent — gives the turn of the tragedy to a pause, and this is what comes out of it: not a decision but a question addressed to the person who made him. 'Unnatural' is the word the play has used for a son marching on his birthplace, and he now applies it to the scene of his surrender.

quotations.text: You have won a happy victory to Rome; But, for your son,--believe it, O, believe it, Most dangerously you have with him prevail'd, If not most mortal to him.
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: Granting the peace his mother has come to ask for.
quotations.analysis: He states the cost accurately and in the same breath as the concession, which is why the scene is not a redemption. The repeated 'believe it' is the only time in the play he begs anyone to listen, and it is addressed to the one person who has never needed persuading of anything.

quotations.text: There is differency between a grub and a butterfly; yet your butterfly was a grub. This Marcius is grown from man to dragon: he has wings; he's more than a creeping thing.
quotations.speaker: Menenius
quotations.context: Back in Rome, telling Sicinius there is no hope of mercy.
quotations.analysis: Menenius has spent the play making people into parts of a body, and now he makes his friend into a different species altogether. The animal ladder that began with curs and scabs in 1.1 ends with a dragon, and the man himself is by this point absent from every scene that discusses him.

quotations.text: Name not the god, thou boy of tears!
quotations.speaker: Aufidius
quotations.context: In Corioli, in front of the Volscian lords, as Coriolanus swears by Mars.
quotations.analysis: Aufidius has watched him for five acts and knows the one word that will work: not traitor, which is a political charge, but boy, which is a charge about his mother. The insult is accurate, which is why it destroys him — he yielded to a woman and he knows Aufidius watched him do it.

quotations.text: Cut me to pieces, Volsces; men and lads, Stain all your edges on me. Boy! false hound! If you have writ your annals true, 'tis there, That, like an eagle in a dove-cote, I Flutter'd your Volscians in Corioli: Alone I did it. Boy!
quotations.speaker: Coriolanus
quotations.context: His last speech, to the citizens of the city he sacked.
quotations.analysis: He answers an insult about his mother by reciting the deed that gave him his name, in the city that gave it, to the survivors of it. 'Alone I did it' is the claim the play has been quietly disputing since 1.6, when an entire army picked him up and carried him — and it is the last thing he says before the conspirators move.

quotations.text: My rage is gone; And I am struck with sorrow. Take him up. Help, three o' the chiefest soldiers; I'll be one.
quotations.speaker: Aufidius
quotations.context: Standing over the body, moments after standing on it.
quotations.analysis: The reversal takes four words, and the practical instruction that follows is what makes it convincing: he stops speaking about himself and starts organising a stretcher party. Shakespeare gives the killer the last rites rather than the family, so the play's final act of tenderness comes from the enemy and not from Rome.

timeline.label: North's translation of Plutarch's Lives
timeline.detail: Thomas North's English version of Amyot's French Plutarch, and the source Shakespeare follows most closely of any he ever used.

timeline.label: North's Plutarch reissued
timeline.detail: A second edition kept the Lives in print and in circulation through Shakespeare's Roman plays.

timeline.label: Shakespeare writes Julius Caesar
timeline.detail: The first of the plays taken from North, and the one that establishes Shakespeare's method of turning Plutarch's prose into verse.

timeline.label: Shakespeare writes Antony and Cleopatra
timeline.detail: Usually dated to 1606 or 1607, and the immediate predecessor of this play in the Roman sequence.

timeline.label: The Midland Revolt
timeline.detail: Risings against enclosure and grain shortage across the midland counties, often linked by scholars to the corn riot with which this play opens.

timeline.label: The play is written
timeline.detail: Generally dated around this year, which makes it Shakespeare's last tragedy.

timeline.label: The King's Men take the Blackfriars
timeline.detail: An indoor playhouse with a smaller, closer audience — a room in which a long silence between two actors can be made to work.

timeline.label: Plague closes the London playhouses
timeline.detail: A closure that ran on well into the following year and disrupted the company's plans for the new theatre.

timeline.label: The First Folio
timeline.detail: The play is printed first among the tragedies, from a manuscript whose stage directions are unusually full.

places.name: Rome
places.note: The Forum, the Capitol and the street: almost every political scene in the play.

places.name: Antium
places.note: Modern Anzio, where Coriolanus arrives in disguise and offers Aufidius his throat. Corioli's own site is not securely known.

places.name: Chaeronea
places.note: Plutarch's home town in Boeotia; his Life of Caius Martius gave the play its plot and much of its wording.

places.name: Northampton
places.note: At the centre of the 1607 midland risings over enclosure and the price of corn, a year or so before the play was written.

places.name: Blackfriars, London
places.note: The indoor playhouse the King's Men took on in 1608, well suited to a tragedy whose turning point is a silence.

criticalViews.summary: The traditional reading takes Coriolanus at his own valuation and finds the fault in him: an aristocratic contempt so complete that it cannot survive contact with ordinary politics.
criticalViews.counter: It has to ignore how much of what he says about flattery and custom the play allows to be true, and how carefully the tribunes' manipulation is staged.

criticalViews.summary: Since the nineteenth century the play has been read as Shakespeare's most direct treatment of the conflict between rich and poor, with the grain riot as its foundation and the tribunes as a genuine constitutional innovation.
criticalViews.counter: Productions in this vein have been claimed by the left and the right with equal confidence, which suggests the text does not settle the argument it stages.

criticalViews.position: A play about a mother and a son
criticalViews.summary: Psychological criticism has concentrated on Volumnia, on a valour she describes as her own creation, and on a hero whose entire public identity collapses the moment his family kneel in front of him.
criticalViews.counter: Read too narrowly, it turns a play with numbered citizens and a working senate into a family drama with a war in the background.

essayQuestions.question: Does the play take the citizens seriously?
essayQuestions.focus: Crowd, class and the grain riot
plan: Begin with 1.1: the demand is specific — corn at their own price — and one of the citizens is allowed to answer Menenius back.
Examine the belly fable as rhetoric: what it concedes, what it evades, and how the crowd receives it.
Show the citizens in 2.3 reasoning about whether they owe him their voices, and then being told what they should have said.
Weigh the mockery of their inconstancy in 2.3 and 4.6 against the evidence of who is steering them each time.
Conclude on whether the play mocks a mob or shows a new political class being formed and immediately managed.

essayQuestions.question: What happens in the silence of 5.3?
essayQuestions.focus: Volumnia's plea and the play's turning point
plan: Set up the scene: two embassies have already failed, and Coriolanus has just declared he will act as if a man were author of himself.
Track the sequence of interruptions — Virgilia's greeting, the boy, the kneeling — and note that he calls himself a dull actor before his mother's long speech begins.
Read Volumnia's argument closely, especially the moment she makes her own body the gate of Rome.
Treat the Folio direction, 'He holds her by the hand, silent', as text: what does an audience watch during it?
Judge whether the yielding is a recovery of humanity, a final obedience, or both at once, using his own statement of the cost.

essayQuestions.question: How does the play use the body?
essayQuestions.focus: Wounds, the belly and the body politic
plan: Start with Menenius's fable and the state imagined as an anatomy with a hoarding centre.
Follow the wounds: Volumnia counting them in 2.1, Rome demanding to see them in 2.3, and what the refusal to display them actually claims.
Consider the food imagery running alongside — famine, surfeit, anger eaten in 4.2.
Bring in the animal ladder, from scabs and curs to the dragon in 5.4, as the body politic seen from above.
End on 5.3, where a mother's womb becomes the last piece of ground between an army and a city.

essayQuestions.question: Is Aufidius a rival, a lover or an executioner?
essayQuestions.focus: Enmity, admiration and the last scene
plan: Set out the pattern of Act I: beaten five times, and vowing in 1.10 to have him by any means, honourable or not.
Read the welcome at Antium in 4.5 for its language, which borrows freely from marriage and dreaming.
Use 4.7 to show admiration turning into arithmetic once the soldiers begin to prefer the newcomer.
Examine the choice of insult in 5.6 — boy, not traitor — and what it reveals about how closely he has been watching.
Finish with 'My rage is gone', and ask what it means that the play gives its last tenderness to the killer.

discussionQuestions: The citizens are given numbers, arguments and changes of mind. Does that make them a mob or a parliament?
Coriolanus will not show his wounds. Is that integrity, shame, or a refusal to let his body be used as evidence?
Volumnia saves Rome and destroys her son in the same speech. Which does the play think she came to do?
The turning point of the tragedy is a stage direction rather than a line. What does that ask of an actor?
Aufidius kills him for using the name Rome gave him. Who does the name belong to by the end?

related.why: The other Roman play built on North's Plutarch, and the other crowd that can be turned round inside a single scene.
Written immediately before, and the opposite case: a soldier undone by appetite rather than by an inability to ask for anything.
The nearest companion piece — a man who leaves his city in fury and takes an enemy's money to punish it.
The earlier tragedy of a man who cannot perform the words a public occasion requires, and loses everything in the first scene for it.
Shakespeare's first Rome, and a useful measure of how far the political writing had travelled by 1608.
